author: Abahlali_3
title: Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer
content:
25 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

Worsening Violence as the Election Comes Closer

Our country is one of the most violent in the world, worse than some war zones. The rate of violence against women and the rate of murders committed by young men against other young men are among the highest in the world. There is violence in the home and in communities, violence from ordinary people, politicians, criminals and the armed forces in service of the state and the rich.

Our country and its people have been deeply damaged by generations of oppression, which has continued into the present for many people, especially the poor. The ANC has never pursued a project of healing, a project of restoring the humanity of our people and our society. They have just made themselves rich, leaving most of us poor and living in a broken society, a broken society in which the poor continue to be ruled with violence.

Things are getting worse. In KwaZulu-Natal armed mobs now parade through the streets accompanied by the police. People have been driven from their homes and livelihoods, assaulted and killed. The rise of the right, including violent fascist organisations, is a matter of grave concern for our movement and all people of good conscience.

As the election approaches, violence is worsening. So far 43 people have been killed, including people from the ANC, IFP and MKP. The political killings that are taking place are another grave concern for our movement. In a free, democratic country everyone should be free to campaign for election without fear. We know very well that the killing will not be confined to politicians. As killing becomes more common, more and more activists will be targeted in the years ahead.

Right now, the atmosphere in Durban is particularly threatening. Political intolerance has reached a fever pitch. The danger can be felt everywhere. Many politicians and parties have been complicit, and none have built a project in support of healing and a just peace. People are being assaulted and sometimes beaten to death in the streets. The political assassinations continue and will continue after the election as the politicians fight for power and money.

While the situation is at its worst in Durban and KwaZulu-Natal, it is moving into other parts of the country. ANC people have been killed in Katlehong.

People are being encouraged to hate, attack and kill as the election comes closer. But elections come and go. Every time there is an election, politicians come into our communities with promises, food and t-shirts and then they leave. We don’t see them until the next election comes. To them we are voting fodder, people who can be lied to and bribed, and not citizens of a democracy, or even just full human beings.

We have had elections for more than thirty years and the poor remain poor and without land, water, sanitation, electricity and housing. Our dignity continues to be vandalised by the state and the organised power of the rich. We continue to live with our suffering. This election will not resolve any of the problems that we face, and yet we are being encouraged to hate, attack and kill, and to support politicians and parties that are encouraging hate and are involved in political violence.

We cannot now glorify elections as the only thing that can resolve our problems and ensure that our dignity as human beings is recognised. Elections can be important, but all our advances as a movement and as a class have come from building our own power, popular democratic power. We must never allow politicians to divide us. We must never be divided by people who only come to our communities to lie to us when they seek power and then leave us poor and oppressed.

After careful discussions, we have agreed to encourage our members, and others who look to our movement for political direction, to vote according to their conscience if they wish to vote, but not to support those who have disappointed and betrayed them in the past, and who have made the poor suffer for more than thirty years. They must not vote for people who are trying to divide the poor with ethnic politics and political intolerance, for the corrupt who steal from the poor or for people who are xenophobic. They must not vote for any politicians or parties that encourage hate and violence.

When this election has passed, the oppressed will remain oppressed, there will be greater political intolerance and our society will be even more violent …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu to campaign for ANC and SACP
content:
Cosatu has pledged to campaign for both the African National Congress (ANC) and the South African Communist Party (SACP) in the upcoming local government elections, warning that its political support will not prevent it from confronting either party if workers’ interests are undermined.


SACP candidates will be contesting the local government polls on 4 November, independently of the ANC for the first time since 1994.


The position emerged from the federation’s 15

th

 national congress, which was held from 12 to 14 October after its

first attempt in September collapsed

. In her first formal press statement as the newly elected general secretary, Zingiswa Losi said the congress reaffirmed Cosatu’s historic mission to organise and mobilise the working class, defend workers’ rights and advance a programme of democratic transformation towards socialism.


The federation’s decision to support both the ANC and SACP followed consultations among affiliates. Losi explained that the unions had adopted positions intended to influence the national congress, which ultimately passed what the leadership called a “super resolution” to support both parties.


The motion to back the SACP was championed by one of Cosatu’s largest affiliates, the National Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu). Losi defended Nehawu and the right of affiliates to consult their constituencies and bring their positions to the congress. She maintained that they had not acted improperly and that the decisive outcome was the congress’s collective resolution supporting both the ANC and SACP. Cosatu’s demands regarding local government, labour rights and public services would apply to both parties. she said.


Congress resolutions


The agenda of Cosatu’s congress involved discussions on the future of organised labour amid mass unemployment, poverty, inequality and rising living costs. The congress acknowledged the need to rebuild Cosatu’s organisational strength and reverse the trend of declining membership in parts of the private sector.


Cosatu’s declared priority is to rebuild workplace structures, organise un-unionised and precariously employed workers, strengthen collective bargaining and to improve accountability among affiliates.


One of the federation’s key proposals is a workers’ cost-of-living index to inform wage negotiations and government policy. Losi argued that economic progress should not be measured simply by declining inflation or headline growth, but by whether workers and their families could afford to live with dignity. “What it costs for workers to live must inform the bargaining strategy,” she said.


The proposed index would assess the weight of food, transport, electricity and healthcare costs on household budgets. Cosatu wants wage negotiations to take into account what money workers have left after meeting essential expenses, particularly when salary increases fail to keep pace with inflation.


The federation is also calling for an expanded basket of zero-rated goods, affordable basic services and the implementation of National Health Insurance to ease the cost of medical care.


Cosatu urged consumers and government to support locally produced goods, arguing that stronger domestic production can help protect manufacturing jobs. The federation maintains that economic growth must translate into employment and improved living standards rather than leave workers trapped in poverty.


Cosatu’s general secretary, Zingiswa Losi campaigning for the ANC in Khayelitsha recently. Photo from Zingiswa Losi’s Facebook page


Cosatu criticises the composition of GNU


While continuing to support the ANC, Cosatu still criticised the composition of the government of national unity, particularly the inclusion of the Democratic Alliance, citing differences over policies such as national health insurance and the national minimum wage. The federation argued that rebuilding the tri-partite alliance with the ANC and SACP must not require workers to accept policies that undermine their interests.


Newly elected president, Mike Shingange stressed that Cosatu’s electoral support was not unconditional. “It doesn’t mean when we campaign and vote for you, and you undermine the interests of the workers, that we’re not going to come for you. We will,” he said.


Shingange said Cosatu would not remain silent if either political partner failed to honour commitments to workers. He warned that their conduct in government could influence the federation’s …

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: N.W.T. premier commits to advancing Dene control of child welfare
content:
Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson says the territorial government will begin discussions with Yellowknives Dene First Nations on formalizing their authority over child and family services, following concerns raised at the Annual Akaitcho Assembly about Indigenous children in care.


Speaking to delegates at the Chief Drygeese Centre on Oct. 28, Simpson said that while Indigenous governments already have the authority to care for their own children, the next step is to begin working toward a coordination agreement between governments under federal legislation.


“In terms of the child welfare piece, we will begin those conversations,” Simpson said. “It’s federal legislation, and it requires an implementation,” said Simpson.


The discussions come as delegates described children being separated from their siblings and communities, families struggling to access services and concerns about whether the child welfare system adequately reflects Indigenous cultures and ways of life.


According to a 2026 federal audit, 98 per cent of children who receive prevention and protection services in the N.W.T. are Indigenous, despite making up only about 58 per cent of the territory’s total child population.


Around the table, delegates said the issue is not only where children are placed, but whether the system supports families, keeps siblings together and allows children to maintain meaningful connections to their language, culture and communities.


Foster care needs more support, delegates say


Jeffery Rosnawski, a delegate, called for stronger oversight of foster homes and more support for Indigenous people who want to become foster caregivers.


“It seems that it’s more like a business. You have a lot of people coming to the north and they’re opening their doors, but they’re getting compensated really well,” Rosnawski said.


He called for ongoing audits to ensure foster homes are meeting children’s needs and not taking advantage of the system for financial gain.


Rosnawski said the issue extends beyond foster homes to the child protection workforce itself. He argued that social workers need a better understanding of the families they serve and that Indigenous representation in the system should reflect the population.


“A lot of our members whose kids are in foster homes they’re going to some of these homes and and you know they’re not even talking English in the homes and they’re not eating the same food that they would if they were in the community,” he said.


He also raised concerns about how families are treated when they are already struggling.


“Sometimes you have to be empathetic and it should be taught,” Rosnawski said, calling for improvements to staff orientation and cultural understanding.


Rosnawski said the territory also needs a family-treatment program so parents working toward reunification can receive support closer to home rather than travelling south and being separated from their communities.


Leaders discuss the child welfare at the annual Akaitcho Assembly. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


‘If we need housing, help us’


Charlie Catholique, a foster parent from Deninu Kųę́First Nation, said he and his wife have cared for more than 30 children since 1999. He told delegates that communities need more resources, including larger homes, to make it possible for local caregivers to take in children who might otherwise be sent away.


He described caring for a young child who had been moved through five homes before reaching his first birthday.


Catholique said children who have experienced trauma need stable homes and caregivers who can offer the support they require. He said his own household has only been able to care for a limited number of children at a time.


“If we need housing, help us. That way more kids will stay home,” he said.


Catholique said children are sometimes sent outside their communities and separated from their siblings because local caregivers cannot accommodate them all.


“They leave the community, go to Edmonton sometimes, right here. And they’re separated. They’re not together. We should be, we should always keep them together,” he said.


He also pushed back against the idea that foster care should be treated as a source of profit. Catholique said caregivers need enough financial and practical support to meet children’s needs, but that caring for children should be rooted in a commitment to them.


His comments point to a practical barrier for communities …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Suggests Ilhan Omar, a US Citizen, Doesn’t Have Constitutional Rights
content:
“She goes, ‘I have constitutional rights.’ The arrogance,” Trump said at a rally in Texas.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

President Donald Trump suggested that Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), a U.S. citizen, should not have constitutional rights because of where she’s from in racist remarks at a rally this week.

“She was from Somalia and she came over and right away she started opening her mouth, ‘I have constitutional rights,’” Trump said mockingly, in the middle of a three-and-a-half minute rant about Omar in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night. “She comes from a country with no government, no counsel, no police, no anything. It’s not even a country. It’s just a piece of land.”

“She goes, ‘I have constitutional rights.’ The arrogance,” Trump said. He then transitioned into making Islamophobic comments about Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Trump has consistently targeted Omar with racist remarks, and has previously called Somalia a “garbage country.”

Trump’s comments on Tuesday suggest that he believes Omar should not be afforded basic rights laid out in the U.S. Constitution, like freedom of speech and religion or the right to a fair trial. Notably, these protections are supposed to apply to everyone within the United States, not just citizens.

Trump has repeatedly remarked on Omar’s right to constitutional protections. He has said some iteration of these comments at many rallies this midterm cycle — including just after Homeland Security Investigations’ pre-dawn raid on her house earlier this month. However, Tuesday’s version is the clearest he’s been about suggesting that Omar doesn’t deserve such rights.

The president’s rant comes as his administration is attempting to denaturalize and deport Omar — part of a mass deportation campaign that critics say has already drastically eroded or is directly violating numerous constitutional liberties.

This is a remarkable rebuke of the Constitution coming from the leader of the party that is attacking people like Omar and El-Sayed as un-American.

Indeed, Republicans in Congress and in Trump’s orbit have repeatedly made comments suggesting that only Christians should be allowed to be in Congress, and that Muslims specifically should be barred from holding office.

At a rally in Ohio on Wednesday night, for instance, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said that El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan, is an “affront to me as a naturalized citizen of this country” and “can be nowhere near D.C.” His reasoning was that El-Sayed doesn’t understand “that our rights come from God Almighty” and that “Jesus came here for our salvation.”

The GOP’s racist and Islamophobic remarks have become increasingly incendiary as the election has neared. On Wednesday, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said that, if El-Sayed were to gain access to classified information, “there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result” — a remark that critics noted was open incitement to violence.

Just days before the raid on Omar’s house, Trump called for a race war against Somalis in Omar’s home state of Minnesota. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said “The people of Minnesota must fight back” against Somali immigrants in the state.

Truthout is funded almost entirely by readers — that’s why we can speak truth to power and cut against the mainstream narrative. But independent journalists at Truthout face mounting political repression under Trump.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: No charges against police involved in fatal 2025 Kangiqsualujjuaq shooting
content:
Quebec’s Director of Criminal and Pénal Prosecutions will not lay charges against a Nunavik Police Service officer who fatally shot a man in Kangiqsualujjuaq in May 2025, finding that the officer was justified in his use of lethal force under the Criminal Code.


The decision follows a review of the investigation conducted by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, according to a release issued by Quebec’s prosecutor’s office Wednesday.


The Nunavik Police Service had been searching for the Mark Annanack since April 5, 2025, after he escaped from custody at the Kangiqsualujjuaq police station.


On May 6, at around 10:25 p.m., officers found him hiding in a tent in a wooded area behind a house. When they approached him, he repeatedly claimed to have a knife and a firearm and threatened to use them, the release said.


Officers tried to persuade him to cooperate. When he attempted to leave the tent, police sprayed him in the face with pepper spray.


At around 10:39 p.m., the man exited the tent again and walked toward an officer. After being told the man had a knife, the officer ordered him to stop and fired two rounds from a Taser, according to the report.


The man remained standing and continued walking toward the officer, who then fired two gun shots.


Annanack, was taken to a health centre, where he was pronounced dead at 11:47 p.m.


A forensic pathologist determined that the death was caused by multiple gunshot wounds, the release said.


The prosecutor’s office found the officer’s use of force was justified under the Criminal Code, which allows police to use lethal force when necessary to protect themselves or others from death or serious bodily harm.


This is the second of four police-involved deaths from the past year and a half to receive a decision on charges.


In August, the prosecutor announced it wouldn’t lay charges against police officers in the death of James Kavik in Inukjuak in July 2025.


Joshua Papigatuk

 died in November 2024 and his twin brother Garnet was badly injured after they were shot by police in Salluit.


Then, in December 2025, a six-year-old girl identified by a family member as Alacie Iqaluk died and her father, Andrew Naluktuk, was injured in a

police-involved shooting

 in Inukjuak.

author: Neesha Powell
title: A North Carolina movement asks voters to reject corporate tax breaks
content:
This article

A North Carolina movement asks voters to reject corporate tax breaks

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


The affordability crisis is hitting people hard across the country, but it’s especially acute in North Carolina. For

the sixth year

 in a row, North Carolina holds the distinction of being the worst state in the nation for workers based on its wage policies, worker protections, and rights to organize, according to Oxfam.

Nearly half of renters

 in the state are struggling to afford their homes, while nearly a third of households are cost-burdened (spending over 30 percent of their income on housing).


North Carolina voters’ eyes may light up when they see

two proposed constitutional amendments

 on their November ballots: one to cap the state personal and corporate income tax rates at 3.5 percent, down from a cap of seven percent, and another to limit how much local governments can levy in property taxes. On their face, they appear as if they might bring much-needed tax relief to North Carolina’s working class. 


The amendments are deceptively framed as being beneficial to working people and homeowners, reading as if they would lower individual taxes when there’s no indication that they will, according to Todd Warren, statewide campaign strategist at Down Home North Carolina, a member-led organization that endorsed a “no” vote. Instead, Warren said, the measures would be a giveaway to corporations and wealthy individuals by limiting how much they pay toward the public good — and a “scam” for voters.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Since the passage of the two Republican-sponsored bills that placed the amendments on the ballot this past May, Down Home NC and over 20 other groups have come together as the

NC Vote Against coalition

 to defeat them, as well as to oppose a third amendment that would enshrine voter identification requirements in the state constitution.


Each organization has its own expertise and its own tactics, but a common message: The amendments will not benefit working-class people, but rather corporations and the ultra-wealthy. Each group is playing its part in collecting a total of 100,000 pledges from North Carolinians who commit to voting against the amendments.


The fight to fund the future


Down Home NC joined together with another coalition member, the Carolina Federation, to launch the

Fund the Future campaign

, deploying nearly 200 paid canvassers.  


Jenn Frye, co–director of the Carolina Federation, spent part of this weekend canvassing at the poll at a Durham, North Carolina library, where she convinced an older couple to vote “no” on the amendments. After a member-led endorsement process that included political education on the amendments, a leadership summit and a vote at a statewide membership meeting, the Carolina Federation decided they wanted to deeply engage in the amendment fight. “We see more and more people in North Carolina who agree that corporations and the wealthiest individuals aren’t contributing what they owe when day in and day out, North Carolinians are working really hard,” Frye said. “We pay our taxes, and we contribute what we owe.”


Down Home NC and the Carolina Federation were founded in 2017 and 2018, respectively, in the wake of President Trump first taking office and Republicans winning control of both North Carolina’s state legislature and governorship in 2013 (for

the first time

 since Reconstruction). The groups share a long-term goal of loosening corporate power’s grip on the state legislature and supplanting it with people power.


The

Fund the Future campaign

 campaign is knocking doors, talking to voters at the polls, getting resolutions against the amendments passed by local governments and school boards, and placing signs in small businesses and in yards, among other tactics. So far, the Carolina Federation’s canvassers have knocked on over 600,000 doors across six counties, collecting over 33,000 pledges, while Down Home NC’s canvassers had knocked 500,000 doors across 20 counties and collected about 8,000 pledges.


“Whatever the outcome of this amendment fight, Federation’s members plan to launch a statewide campaign next year with other organizations like Down Home and

Siembra

 to demand that the legislature pass fair tax policies that make corporations and the wealthiest individuals pay what they owe our communities in taxes,” Frye …

author: Madelyn Amos
title: ¡Sí Se Puede!: Dolores Huerta’s Feminist Legacy Lives On
content:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader, civil rights activist, and feminist who devoted her life to advancing equality and justice, has died at the age of 96. Her groundbreaking work reshaped the labor and feminist movements, leaving an enduring legacy of grassroots organizing, women’s leadership, and collective action that continues to inspire generations.

Huerta was a dear friend and ally of the Feminist Majority Foundation since its founding. She served on the organization’s board for more than 30 years, offering her passion, energy, and visionary leadership to the fight for gender equality.

In the 1980s, Feminist Majority co-founders Eleanor Smeal and Kathy Spillar recruited Huerta to join the Feminization of Power campaign to increase women’s representation in elected office. For four years, Huerta traveled across the country with the Feminist Majority. She mentored women running for office, particularly Latinas and other women of color, and helped them secure endorsements while campaigning alongside them.

Reflecting on their work together, Smeal recalled, “We traveled to 8 states and she was determined to change the composition of California’s state legislature — and she did. When we started the campaign in 1987, the state legislature was only 14.2% women, but because of Dolores, it quickly jumped to 24.2%. And today, the California legislature is 49.2% women.” Now, in Congress, women are 42% of congressional Democrats, getting closer and closer to parity every year.

Spillar added in her memories of the tour with Huerta, “We would gather women active in their communities in their living rooms and talk about the need for more women to run for office. Dolores would always say to them ‘if you can’t recruit someone, then one of you has to step forward and run.’”

Huerta’s tireless organizing helped build momentum for a historic increase in women’s political representation, culminating in the 1992 election widely known as the “Year of the Woman.”

Smeal continued, “She would just keep going, it didn’t matter if it was midnight or 2am. She was my kind of person and we would just stay up all night strategizing. She worked day in and day out for women’s rights, labor rights, civil rights, LGBTQ rights, environmentalism — she was a leader in all the key issues. Her passion was infectious and inspiring.”

Smeal remembers a conversation with Huerta about the lasting impact of their activism. Huerta told her, “Our daughters can have a very different life than us because of the work we did.” Her work will live on in the movements she helped build and the generations who will carry her legacy forward.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Manitoba, community protests legislation that would fast-track resource projects: ‘Have we not lost enough?’
content:
About 100 people attended a demonstration outside the Manitoba legislature on Saturday, ahead of Monday’s First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting where Bill C-39 was on the agenda in Ottawa. Photo by Crystal Greene


Indigenous people in Manitoba are protesting against proposed federal legislation that aims to fast-track resource development — saying it undermines their rights and sovereignty over their lands.


Activists point to several pieces of legislation that they worry would cause more harm to their territories, which are already impacted by climate change and the biodiversity crisis. They also have safety concerns over “man camps” created by industry and potential harms to vulnerable Indigenous women and girls.


Both

Bill C-5

 and

Bill C-39

 are set to fast-track major infrastructure projects in “Canada,” by designating them to be of “national interest.” C-5 was passed in 2025, and C-39 is in its third reading. Meanwhile, the proposed

Bill C-37

 — under review after a second reading — has heightened concerns over First Nations water rights. 


One such

project of “national interest”

 is

Churchill Plus

. It would see a pipeline and terminal built to internationally export LNG through the Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay. The arctic deepwater seaport would also handle increased mining exports out of Manitoba, eventually including the

Ring of Fire

.


About 20 people gathered outside of the Manitoba Legislature on Monday rallying against the legislation and in response to the First Nations-first ministers meeting in Ottawa, which was part of similar solidarity events that happened across “Canada.”


It was one of a few protests in Manitoba in late October against the bills and the extractive projects being pushed through by colonial governments despite opposition. 


People who once stood together in the same spot – the Manitoba legislature – during Idle No More, are standing together again to oppose the fast tracking of major infrastructure projects. Photo by Crystal Greene


Alex Wilson

 of Opaskwayak Cree Nation, a professor in the Faculty of Education at the University of Winnipeg, and an organizer with Idle No More, was at Monday’s rally outside the legislature


Wilson read

a collective statement from Idle No More

 founders that said “the conditions that gave rise to Idle No More in 2012 are confronting us again.”


Wilson said that includes “sweeping legislative changes, threats to environmental protections, and government decisions affecting Indigenous territories without respecting the authority of the people who belong to those lands.”


Wilson told IndigiNews that there’s been “a constant erosion of treaty rights of Indigenous sovereignty and legislation that protects land, water and the sky.”


“The bills that are proposed are kind of galvanising our understanding that this is an agenda that is continually harming First Nations, Indigenous peoples and our environment.”


At another earlier rally at the Manitoba legislature, on Saturday, Indigenous activists and allies spoke against Bills C-39 and C-37.  It was a finale of the

Arctic Crossroads Tour

 in Manitoba that visited Churchill, Nisichawayasihk, Thompson, Brandon, and Winnipeg.


Anishinaabe water protector Taylor Galvin who works closely with Manitoba First Nations that are impacted by hydro projects on their lands, attended the event.


Taylor Galvin spoke during Saturday’s event to oppose Bills C-37 and C-39 outside the Manitoba legislature. Photo by Crystal Greene


“Have we not lost enough? We are living in a ticket time bomb, and our lands and our waters don’t have time, and in Manitoba, our sturgeon relatives don’t have time,” said Galvin, who is from Baaskaandibewi-ziibiing (Brokenhead Ojibway Nation).


“Our fish and our waters are already sick, traces of life-threatening metals like mercury, lead, arsenic, and cadmium are being found in those fish and in those waters.”


Galvin spoke of political greed and “a broken system” that has harmed the environment and continues to extract from it.


“We have a broken system and yet they want more, Bill C-39, removing Indigenous rights, and trying to move forward at a very quick pace for projects of ‘national interest,’” Galvin said.


“Why aren’t the people considered national interests? What aren’t the animals considered national interests? Why are they talking about these things without protecting anything?”

title: Private Prison Companies Are Pouring Money Into GOP Coffers Ahead of Midterms
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


PACs and executives from three of the leading private prison companies have donated close to $1.2 million to candidates, fundraising committees, and political party committees during this year’s midterm election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records.


A GEO Group subsidiary, GEO Reentry Services LLC,

donated

 an

additional $4.4 million

 to MAGA Inc.,

a super PAC

 supporting President Donald Trump.


Trump’s second term, along with the backing of a Republican-controlled House and Senate, has been a financial boon to the private prison industry. Since Trump took office again, private prison companies CoreCivic and GEO Group

have received

 more than $1 billion in contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) As of July, there were

close to 59,000 people

 detained by ICE, the

majority of whom

 are held in privately run immigration jails.


Truthout

 reviewed campaign contributions made by three private prison company PACs — CoreCivic, GEO Group, and Management & Training Corporation (MTC) — as well as donations made by their executives for the 2025-2026 election cycle. We examined donations made for the primary and general elections, to PACs directly controlled by the candidates, campaign fundraising committees, and donations to entities like the Republican National Committee. For executives, we only included donations over $1,000.


Truthout

’s review of FEC records reveals that:


The three private prison PACs

donated

 about $774,000 during the midterm election cycle, including a total of $320,000 to the Republican National Committee, the National Republican Congressional Committee, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC.)


GEO Group’s PAC outspent CoreCivic and MTC’s PACs, with donations totaling about $456,000.


Executives from CoreCivic and GEO Group

donated

Truthout

While the overwhelming majority of private prison donations went to Republicans, there were a handful of donations to Democrats. MTC’s PAC

donated $2,000

 to Mississippi Democratic Congressman Bennie Thompson’s campaign, and CoreCivic’s PAC

donated $5,000

 to Texas Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar’s Texas First

leadership PAC

. CoreCivic’s PAC

donated $1,000

 to the Montana Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, in addition to the $3,000 donated to the Montana Republican Legislative Campaign Committee.


Among the top recipients of private prison cash were

Congressman Andrew Garbarino

 (R-New York) and

Sen. Ashley Moody

 (R-Florida). Garbarino is the chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security and Moody is on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security, as noted in a recent report by

Scripps News

.


CoreCivic, GEO Group, and MTC’s PACs donated a total of $30,000 to Garbarino’s campaign, but the FEC records reviewed did not show any donations from CoreCivic or GEO Group executives.

GEO Group’s PACs

 and

executives

joint fundraising committee

 for her campaign and the NRSC. CoreCivic’s PAC donated $1,000 to her campaign. The super PAC

Stronger Safer Nation

, which supports Moody, also received a donation of $20,000 from GEO Reentry Services.


Moody is a Trump loyalist who, as Florida’s attorney general,

joined

 Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s

efforts to overturn

 the 2020 presidential election results.


Moody is running against Democrat Angie Nixon, a current state representative, in a race that has drawn national attention. Nixon, who is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America,

secured an upset primary victory

 in August. Sen. Bernie Sanders

has joined Nixon

 on the campaign trail, and

former President Barack Obama

 and

Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

Truthout

title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Trailer Has Sapphic Sex and Sad Exes
content:
Season one of The Hunting Wives was a wild ride, and I have a feeling season two is going to be even wilder. The full trailer dropped and it has me clapping and kicking my feet at the sapphic chaos about to descend upon us.

The trailer opens with Sophie’s husband asking if Sophie is “still dreaming about her” (“her” being Margo) and a few flashing scenes implies that yes, yes she is.

Other things we see flash by: a glam cowgirl photo shoot, Margo being manipulative to all kinds of people, and Callie being a sad ex and using a photo of Margo as target practice.

This show also knows exactly what it is and is leaning into it. For example, the song playing is Nancy Sinatra’s “Bang Bang”, which is the perfect backdrop for this trailer full of guns and sex and chaos. And the tagline for the season is “someone is going down,” which the narrator says while the visuals cut between a dead body and also a more…explicit interpretation of the phrase.

Based on how season one ended, I can’t wait to find out how Sophie ends up back in Margo’s bed (and her bubble bath!), and luckily we only have one month left to wait.

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Fraser Needham
title: Columnist says more pressing issues on agenda at First Nations meeting than abolishing Indian Act
content:
A columnist with the Hill Times says a First Nations meeting with First Ministers this week was not the appropriate venue to be discussing abolishing the more than a century-and-a-half old Indian Act.

“It seems to me that a lot of things were said at mics on that day that people really regret,” Rose LeMay said. “I don’t know anyone who would disagree that the Indian Act has to go. It’s a racist piece of segregationist law. It always has been. Whether we take out a clause here or there it’s still fundamentally a barrier to human rights. Especially for First Nations women. We’ve seen all the debate on S-2 and trying to bring in the one parent instead of the second-generation cut-off. Overall, it’s a piece of racist legislation. Was that day the day to raise it? I don’t think so.”

Lemay said it is her understanding that much more time in the meeting was spent on discussing how the government’s proposed Bill C-39 – the Building Canada Strong Act – could affect First Nations rights when it comes resource development.

She also said more pressing issues including First Nations access to health care and systemic discrimination against First Nations women should have been given more of a focus by government ministers in post meeting media scrums.

The meeting, which took place on Monday in Ottawa, was the first time First Nations leaders had their own table with the prime minister and provincial and territorial premiers.

The idea of abolishing the Indian Act was first raised by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew during a press scum and later brought up again by Prime Minister Mark Carney during his closing statements at the meeting.

APTN News online journalist Karyn Pugliese said one of the more interesting discussions to come out of it was talk of making changes to the Natural Resources Transfer Agreement to include First Nations.

“The Natural Resources Transfer Agreement was signed in 1930 by which the federal government gave resources to the provinces,” she said. “So, this is to say, the provinces own resources like oil and minerals but First Nations were never consulted on that and chiefs would be quick to say they never gave up these resources and so they were there to raise the issue.”

First Nations in provinces who are part of the NRTA – Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta – have long argued they should receive a percentage of resource revenue royalties that these provinces currently collect solely for themselves.

The issue has once again risen to the fore as the Carney government pushes ahead on resource development projects while at the same time saying First Nations should be part of and benefit from these projects.

Nearly 200 First Nations leaders, the prime minister and premiers gathered for a historic meeting about almost everything. Now what?

A veteran Native American journalist says Native American women are running in some of the key races in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

“Two of the candidates are favoured – in Minnesota Penny Flanagan and Mary Peltola in Alaska,” Mark Trahant said. “And I think it’s curious that when the first Native women were elected to the U.S. House of Representatives – which included Deb Haaland who’s running for governor – it was two, it wasn’t one. And at the time I remember writing that two made all the difference in the world because they play off of each other, they could not have to be everywhere together. And I think that same sort of thing is important for the Senate because being two will allow them to basically come up with a strategy rather than being the only and isolated as such.”

Flanagan and Peltola are running as Democrats for Senate seats.

A third Native American woman, N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, is also running for the Democrats seeking a Senate seat in Oklahoma.

A Native American woman has never been elected to the U.S. Senate.

Deb Haaland, a former of secretary of the interior under President Joe Biden, is running for governor as a Democrat in New Mexico.

The midterm elections take place on Tuesday.

He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: Rosa Amorim: "Hablar de reforma agraria en Brasil es hablar de un proyecto de dignidad de vida"
content:
“Com a barriga vazia não consigo dormir,

E com o bucho mais cheio, comecei a pensar.

Que eu me organizando posso desorganizar

Que eu desorganizando posso me organizar

Que eu me organizando posso desorganizar”.

Da lama ao caos, Nação Zumbi - Chico Science


“Con la panza vacía no puedo dormir,

Con el buche más lleno, empecé a pensar.

Que desorganizándome puedo organizar

Que organizando me puedo desorganizar

Que desorganizándome puedo organizar”


Por Mariángeles Guerrero y Carla Perelló

Desde Brasil


Rosa Amorim es la primera mujer del Movimiento de los Trabajadores Rurales sin Tierra (MST) en ser electa diputada nacional en Brasil. Es negra, lesbiana, oriunda de Pernambuco, nordeste del país, y tiene 29 años. Integra el Partido de los Trabajadores (PT). Durante la pandemia, mientras gobernaba Jair Bolsonaro, fue una de las impulsoras de la red de cocinas solidarias que enfrentaron el hambre en los barrios populares de las ciudades. La reelección de Lula da Silva significa una victoria popular y una esperanza, pero la conformación de un Congreso con mayoría de la extrema derecha plantea sus propios desafíos. En ese escenario, sostiene que la “lucha parlamentaria” será vital. “Queremos que Brasil deje de ser uno de los países que más venenos y agrotóxicos consume”, afirma.


Hija de la lucha por la reforma agraria, Amorim creció en las filas del MST y también fue dirigente estudiantil. Desde sus orígenes, el movimiento campesino mantuvo su autonomía aunque apoyó candidaturas del PT. Pero, en 2022, tras el retroceso en materia de derechos que significó el gobierno de Jair Bolsonario, presentó sus propios candidatos. Ese año, ella fue electa diputada del estado de Pernambuco.

El pasado 5 de octubre fue electa diputada nacional; una de lxs 38 legisladorxs LGBT+ que obtuvieron un escaño y una de los cuatro integrantes del MST que estarán en el Congreso brasileño

.


En el histórico proceso electoral que consolidó a Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva como presidente por los próximos cuatro años, Amorim fue una de las jóvenes que acompañó la campaña para revertir la derrota que el PT obtuvo en la primera vuelta.

Llevará las banderas de la reforma agraria y la soberanía alimentaria al Poder Legislativo. Allí el agronegocio presiona, de la mano de la bancada ruralista, para obtener beneficios y seguir extendiendo la frontera agropecuaria

, causando deforestación y contaminación.


En contraste, el MST lleva cuatro décadas de lucha por la tierra para la producción de alimentos sanos.

“Alimentamos al pueblo porque con comida en la panza podemos tener mentes pensantes y con mentes pensantes podemos organizarnos”

, sostuvo en entrevista con Tierra Viva, haciendo honor a la histórica banda nordestina Nação Zumbi liderada por Chico Science.


Foto: Prensa PT


Las cocinas solidarias, que define como “una tecnología social para organizar al pueblo”, se convirtieron en política pública en 2023, durante el gobierno de Da Silva. Su objetivo es vincular el campo con la ciudad, llevando alimentos sanos a espacios comunitarios de los barrios populares. En esos ámbitos se brinda un plato de comida pero también escucha, alfabetización, contención y cuidados. Para la diputada, comer es el primer paso para cuestionar por qué existe el hambre y la pobreza.


—¿En qué situación está hoy la soberanía alimentaria en Brasil?

—Hablar del hambre no es solamente hablar de si el pueblo come por la mañana, por la tarde y por la noche. Es más profundo. Combatir el hambre también significa hablar de la calidad de lo que se come. Y para eso vamos a tener que librar una lucha muy grande. Ya la estamos librando, pero va a ser todavía mayor: la lucha contra el agronegocio, contra el modelo de producción vigente que hace que las personas se enfermen por lo que consumen todos los días. Queremos que Brasil deje de ser uno de los países que más venenos y agrotóxicos consume. Y esto tiene una relación directa con la lucha parlamentaria. Vamos a tener que librar una enorme disputa contra el agronegocio en el Congreso para reducir la cantidad de agrotóxicos que se autorizan en Brasil. También vamos a tener que poner en la agenda la ampliación de las tierras cultivables destinadas a la agricultura familiar y campesina.

Llego al Congreso Nacional para conformar y construir la bancada de la tierra, de la agricultura familiar y de la agricultura campesina. Queremos debatir cómo combatir el hambre y qué estamos consumiendo en Brasil.

Tenemos que debatir la …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Santiago del Estero: Corrupción y desalojo contra comunidad originaria La Armonía
content:
Un operativo policial intentó desalojar este miércoles a una familia del territorio ancestral de la comunidad indígena Lule Vilela La Armonía, en el Departamento Copo de la provincia de Santiago del Estero, a instancias de una persona ajena a la comunidad, Isabel Salas, que reclama la tierra comunitaria como propia y pretende venderla. La resistencia frenó el desalojo y la orden fue temporalmente suspendida.


Intento de desalojo en la comunidad La Armonía. Captura de video de MOCASE VC


“Así es el atropello para desalojar a campesinos indígenas de la comunidad indígena Lule Vilela La Armonía”, denunció el Movimiento Campesino de Santiago del Estero (MOCASE) Vía Campesina al publicar un video del despliegue policial ocurrido durante la mañana de este miércoles 28 de octubre.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por MOCASE VC (@mocase_viacampesina)


“Así es la mafia de la venta ilegal de tierras a los que les gusta la plata”, agregaron desde la organización, y responsabilizaron a una persona llamada Isabel Salas, alias “Chabela”, de la localidad de Monte Quemado, como la impulsora del operativo. Desde la comunidad La Armonía agregaron que se trata de una situación repetida, y que Isabel Salas “le paga al Oficial de Justicia”.


Vender el territorio ancestral


Rosa Córdoba, Consejera de la Comunidad Lule Vilela La Armonía, detalló la situación que están enfrentando: “Hemos sufrido un atropello aquí en la comunidad, en el lugar denominado 5 Hermanos donde vive la familia Tévez y Salto. La familia está conformada con 5 hijos, nietos, yerno, nueras. Ellos viven de hace más de 10 años en el lugar, pero es territorio relevado, ancestral de la comunidad. Como la comunidad siempre ha tenido una idea de eso, de los territorios que están relevados y vacíos, que se le den a hijos de compañeros del lugar, y esto ha sucedido así”.

Audio: Rosa Córdoba


El campesinado santiagueño, criollo e indígena,

sufre históricamente situaciones de violencia e indefensión jurídica y social

 ante sujetos que buscan apropiarse de tierras comunales y fiscales, muchas veces con la complicidad activa y manifiesta de funcionarios judiciales y de las fuerzas de seguridad.


Así ocurre en este caso. Rosa cuenta que “esta mujer, Isabel Salas, alias Chabela, conjuntamente con su hijo, Federico Guzmán, se quieren apropiar del lugar diciendo que es de ellos, y tan solo se quieren apropiar para venderlo. Ya esta mujer lo ha vendido varias veces haciendo esas solicitudes truchas, que desde Colonización

(nota: se refiere a la ex

Dirección de Colonización

 de Santiago del Estero)

, lo sabía hacer a estas solicitudes que se le daba a cualquiera y en cualquier lugar, sin importarle quién viviese en el territorio ese. Entonces, estas personas vendían esos lugares a cordobeses, a chaqueños, y ellos se iban apropiando así de los lugares. Entonces, llega esta mujer queriendo vender cierta cantidad de hectáreas que dice que son 3200 hectáreas, que es territorio ancestral de la comunidad”.


Intento de desalojo en la comunidad La Armonía. Captura de video de MOCASE VC


La resistencia frenó el desalojo


“Nosotros estamos organizados con el MOCASE en la comunidad La Armonía, y nos despertamos con esta noticia”, contó Rosa.


“En realidad, no nos despertamos porque todos aquí estamos trabajando en las tareas laborales en el campo, y todo el mundo se ha puesto alerta, dejando lo que teníamos que hacer, por ir a solidarizarse con el compañero para que no sea desalojado. Entonces, ahí nos damos que todo ha sido arreglado, como esta mujer le paga al Oficial de Justicia, le paga a la Policía de Santiago del Estero para que haga este desalojo”.


“Entonces, aquí, como nosotros vamos al lugar y comenzamos a resistir en el lugar, a decir que no lo van a desalojar al compañero, porque el lugar es de la comunidad, es del compañero, está produciendo en el lugar. Que nos oponíamos a todo eso. Entonces, al ver toda esta resistencia de la comunidad que hubo, el juez dictamina que se cancele el desalojo y que hagan todo un inventario y que hagan una investigación profunda”.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Solidão “premium”: como redes sociais e consumo transformam estar só em desejo
content:
No Pauta Pública desta semana, Andrea Dip recebe Lucas Liedke e André Alves, psicanalistas, pesquisadores e fundadores da Float Vibes, instituto de estudos culturais e pesquisa comportamental. Apresentadores do podcast Vibes em Análise, eles discutem como as redes sociais transformam a noção de coletividade e de individualidade e como as empresas por trás dessas plataformas se beneficiam da solidão. Para Lucas, o consumidor solitário tende a ser mais rentável para o mercado. 


Segundo um

relatório

 da Organização Mundial da Saúde, uma em cada seis pessoas no mundo se sente sozinha, com impactos significativos na saúde e no bem-estar. Para os entrevistados, as redes sociais prometem conexão e pertencimento, mas também podem intensificar o avanço da solidão entre as pessoas e transformar em espetáculo. “Quem filma a solidão […] no limite também está colocando a câmera como testemunha, ou a suposta audiência como testemunha… um artifício para não estar exatamente sozinho”, resume André Alves. Para Lucas Liedke, este é exatamente o ponto de atenção, já que as plataformas lucram com essa dinâmica. “O imaginário divertido e hipersocial das mídias sociais pode ser opressor”.


As redes sociais não só contribuem para este fenômeno como podem transformá-lo em uma espécie de espetáculo. 


Leia os principais pontos da conversa e ouça o podcast completo abaixo.


EP 239


											A solidão “premium” – com Vibes em Análise


23 de outubro de 2026


					·


				Psicanalistas do Vibes em Análise falam sobre o aumento da solidão e como as redes transformaram a ideia de coletividade


0:00


-:–


15


15


Veja mais episódios desta série


Vocês escreveram esse texto, Solidão Premium, que é uma análise sobre muitos temas que se entrelaçam. Então pra começar, o que é a solidão premium?


Lucas Liedke:

 A discussão sobre solidão vem acontecendo enquanto sintoma global há algum tempo. Com certeza com mais força há uns cinco anos, a partir da pandemia, do trabalho remoto, do isolamento social. Alguns fenômenos que já eram uma realidade, mas que foram ganhando expansão, se tornando uma necessidade e nós sabemos que muitas pessoas nunca conseguiram voltar ao que era antes.


No Japão tem esse fenômeno do

hikikomori

, que são os indivíduos que não saem de casa, de forma alguma, e ficam nesse confinamento extremo. Na China, a gente viu o lançamento de um aplicativo, que tem um nome bastante macabro, que é

Você Está Morto?

, onde as pessoas são convidadas a fazer um check-in a cada dois dias para mostrar para as outras que elas ainda estão vivas.


Nesse contexto, a gente começou a perceber um movimento também de influenciadores de solidão. Pessoas que afirmam ter um um orgulho de não ter uma família próxima, de não ter muitos amigos, de passar um sábado à noite sozinho em casa, assistindo o que quiser no streaming, comendo o que quiser no delivery, sem ter que negociar os seus gostos, as suas escolhas com ninguém. E isso é um contraste curioso para as redes sociais, que sempre foi um lugar mais de expor o quanto você é sociável, o quanto você se diverte, as suas conexões, enquanto uma espécie de capital social. Essa contradição foi o que nos levou a escrever esse texto “Solidão Premium”.


André Alves:

 Tem o famoso relatório da

OMS de 2025

 sobre como uma em cada seis pessoas no mundo se sente afetada pela solidão. Sob à luz da psicanálise – que é o campo de onde a gente parte – a definição da solidão parte de uma espécie de déficit relacional. “Eu não tenho quantitativamente e ou qualitativamente relações suficientes na minha vida”. Claro que nunca a gente tem a suficiência na psicanálise, a gente está sempre trabalhando exatamente com ausências e faltas, mas no caso da epidemia de solidão, é algo que diz sobre faltar demais, sobre eu não ter relações profundas o suficiente, e/ou pessoas o suficiente na minha vida com quem eu possa trocar e que considerem a minha dor como algo importante.


A Solidão Premium, da qual a gente tem falado e esse texto que o Lucas escreveu, parte da ideia de que, no estado atual desse movimento, a gente tem observado muitos criadores de conteúdo, e não só, mas também outras áreas da cultura e da vida de uma forma geral, promovendo uma espécie de estetização da solidão. Um

rebranding

 da solidão: a solidão passando a ser algo ou um estado não só difícil, vergonhoso, culposo, negativo, mas também como um estado aspiracional, algo que eu quero ter na minha vida, pertencer, e acho que dá para a …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Contrainformación anarquista: construir nuestros propios espacios frente a la represión cibernética y las redes sociales
content:
Los medios de comunicación anárquicos han sido fundamentales para expresar, articular, sostener y profundizar nuestros propósitos y proyectos. Por su importancia se han convertido en herramientas imprescindibles y decisivas para la difusión. Sin embargo, existen aspectos que, con el paso del tiempo, pueden ser positivos o disgregar el entramado que los sostiene.

A comienzos del siglo XX, los principales canales de comunicación eran la oratoria, el teatro, la prensa escrita y la fotografía. Lxs agitadorxs avivaban, mediante la voz y la presencia pública, las ideas y prácticas buscando contagiar a lxs demás. Emma Goldman pronunciándose frente a un extenso grupo de personas el 21 de mayo de 1916 en Nueva York constituye una imagen de aquel espíritu que, dispuesto a irrumpir en los espacios, convertía la palabra en acción. La publicación de periódicos también fue esencial para una comunicación orientada a la difusión y al aprendizaje antiautoritario. En 1908, Tierra Libre expresaba que “el periódico es la acción más firme para la propaganda, la defensa y aun el ataque”.

Ya en el siglo XXI, esos canales se transformaron con la incorporación de materiales audiovisuales, sitios web y plataformas digitales. El acceso a la tecnología impulsó a muchxs compañerxs y proyectos anarquistas a incursionar en esta virtualidad. Durante los primeros años aumentó la creación, proyección y circulación de blogs dedicados a noticias, reivindicaciones, actividades, convocatorias y otros contenidos. Pero, ese impulso comenzó a perder fuerza o a desviarse ante la aparición constante de nuevas plataformas más masivas. Los blogs fueron desplazados o quedaron parcialmente superpuestos por la creciente centralidad de Instagram, Twitter y Facebook.

Esta transformación forma parte de un debate que se remonta, al menos, al año 2007, cuando el blog Palabras de Guerra anunció su cierre y denunció “algunos de estos males asociados a internet y propios de la sociedad moderna”. Trece años después, el blog español La Rebelión de las Palabras también decidió abandonar su actividad, debido a la sensación de ajenidad y a la indiferencia experimentada dentro de los entornos anarquistas. Sus editores señalaban que casi nadie se interesaba en enviar convocatorias y reivindicaciones al blog si estas no circulaban previamente por las redes sociales:

“El hecho de que la mayor parte de proyectos en el estado español (centros sociales, ateneos, locales anarquistas o no específicamente anarquistas, pero sí afines a unas fórmulas de auto-organización y un planteamiento autónomo y combativo, colectivos diversos, individualidades…) hayan dejado de utilizar herramientas como este blog para difundir sus proyecciones nos hace pensar que ya no considera estas herramientas como suyas, sino que de algún modo hemos ocupado una esfera de lo ajeno. Cuando vemos que esos mismos colectivos cercanos en la geografía priorizan —cuando no utilizan en exclusiva— las redes sociales como Facebook o Twitter…”[1].

En una fecha cercana, el blog de contrainformación Aleva decidió hacer una pausa. Al retomarlo, sus integrantes explicaron que lo hacían con la convicción de que estos formatos -los sitios web- siguen siendo necesarios para comunicarnos y tienen mucho que aportar a los entornos anarquistas. No eran ingenuos al tomar esa decisión: sabían que las redes sociales habían transformado nuestra manera de leer, de buscar, de establecer expectativas e incluso de definir aquello a lo que estamos dispuestxs a renunciar[2]. Al profundizar en el alcance de esas transformaciones, el blog A las Barricadas difundió una carta con una reflexión relevante:

“Pasamos de la fijación —que algunos aún mantenemos— por el anonimato y disolución de la autoría a ser etiquetados en fotografías que nunca quisimos vieran la luz (…) Cada vez más nos preocupa la pérdida de memoria militante, esto es, la práctica imposibilidad de tener un listado somero de las cosas que realmente hacíamos o la posibilidad de encontrar aquel dato, aquella charla que uno recordaba entre el tráfago absoluto de las redes.”[3]

Coincidimos en que la exposición permanente ha profundizado la pérdida de un sentido iconoclasta de la realidad; es decir, la capacidad de romper con las imágenes y los estereotipos impuestos. La idolatría de las representaciones ha alcanzado incluso nuestros cuerpos, del mismo modo en que antiguamente se rendía culto a una autoridad sagrada. Nos exponemos más de la cuenta para reafirmar quiénes somos …

author: Andrés
title: Agenda cultural, últimos días de octubre
content:
Yo soy el monstruo

, obra de Candelaria Frías. Y escena de

 La Anticrista

, obra de Gonzalo Demaría.


La juventud siempre estuvo despierta. Y ahora también salió a atender a las políticas de ahogo que las generaciones precedentes le están queriendo dejar. Este viernes se podrá ver por última vez la obra de Candelaria Frías,

Yo soy el monstruo

. Y este sábado es el último día para ver

Al fin solos

, que son cinco

solos de danza muy bellamente curados.

Tenemos el bolsillo más flaco del mundo, las ganas desahuciadas, pero salir nos fortalece. Ocupemos las calles. Hay mucho para hacer, gratuito o a precios módicos. R

ecorré nuestra agenda. Elegí compartir cultura. Si tenés propuestas, podés enviarlas a nuestor mail: culturasanred@gmail.com. Revisam

os la casilla hasta el

lunes previo a la publicación.

Por ANRed.


Jueves 29


Cementerio Club.

Lanzamiento de un nuevo sello discográfico que tiene como fin resucitar joyas perdidas. Buenos Aires y Berlín se unen para crear Cementerio Club de la mano de Jay Low. Un nuevo sello que contará con un catálogo atemporal, haya nacido en un estudio casero de los años ochenta o en uno digital del presente. Aquí, su primer lanzamiento: «Trulepa» de Mimilocos, grabado en 1986 y prácticamente inhallable durante casi cuarenta años.

A todo el disco aquí.


XIV edición del festival Internacional Va Poesía Argentina

 se realizará entre el 19 y el 30 de octubre en Mendoza y Buenos Aires. A pesar del contextoeconómico, los directores del Festival, Marta Miranda y Ricardo Rojas Ayrala, volvieron aapostar al encuentro y a la construcción democrática.


Annemarie

.

 El documental de 

Mariana Sanguinetti

, bisnieta de la fotógrafa 

Annemarie Heinrich

, se sumerge en la vida y obra de esta pionera, autora de algunos de los retratos más emblemáticos de la cultura nacional. A través de su archivo, testimonios familiares y la obra de Heinrich, la directora emprende una búsqueda que trasciende el retrato de una artista para convertirse en una reflexión íntima sobre la memoria, la familia, el paso del tiempo y la propia mirada. Una película sobre una fotógrafa, pero también sobre los vínculos que construyen una vida. Estreno en

MALBA Cine

, en octubre.


Borges y México.

La exposición organizada por la

Biblioteca Nacional y la Embajada de México en Argentina

 con la colaboración especial de la

Fundación Internacional Jorge Luis Borges

 da cuenta de una relación de ida y vuelta. Amistades, influencias, afinidades y homenajes que, durante más de 60 años, construyeron un vínculo que trasciende los nombres. Una identidad cultural común entre Argentina y México, una forma de entender la literatura y un modo de habitar la lengua. A partir de libros, fotografías y objetos, la exposición explora la amistad con

Alfonso Reyes

, las coincidencias con

Juan Rulfo

, los viajes a México -en 1973, 1978 y 1981- y las muchas demostraciones de respeto y admiración del pueblo mexicano por Jorge Luis Borges. 

Borges y México

 se puede visitar hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2026; lunes a viernes de 9 a 21 hs. y sábados y domingos de 12 a 19 hs. en la Sala Leopoldo Marechal de la Biblioteca Nacional, Agüero 2502, CABA.


Viernes 30


La bestia soy yo.

De la enfermedad neurológica que provoca un dolor tan grande en la cabeza, que se denomina enfermedad de los suicidas, Candelaria Frías construye una obra que escribe, actúa y dirige.

Los neurólogos

 cuando se refieren a ella,

hablan de “la bestia”

. En esta obra

la Bestia se personifica

, ataca. Y su víctima camina

 entre la vida y la muerte

.  Ante el dolor, el suicidio en brazos del director fue una opción para su autora, pero un encuentro místico torció su destino.

author: Rizomatica
title: Documental sobre el estallido social dirigido por María Teresa Larraín llega a la UCT el 5 de noviembre
content:
Cuerpos en Crisis sigue a cinco activistas durante el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente de 2021-2022 en Chile. La función es de entrada liberada y contará con un conversatorio abierto a la comunidad.


El jueves 5 de noviembre, a las 17:00 hrs, se presentará en Temuco Cuerpos en Crisis, el nuevo documental de la cineasta chileno-canadiense María Teresa Larraín. La actividad, de entrada liberada, se realizará en el Auditorio H2 del Campus San Francisco de la Universidad Católica de Temuco y es organizada por el Observatorio Ciudadano, con el patrocinio del Departamento de Sociología, Ciencia Política y Administración Pública de la UCT.


Tras la exhibición habrá un conversatorio con la directora y con la abogada y ex convencional constituyente mapuche Rosa Catrileo, moderado por Mabel Cobos, codirectora del Observatorio Ciudadano.


La película registra el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente a través de cinco activistas de los movimientos de la discapacidad, migrantes, diversidades sexo-genéricas y personas privadas de libertad. También participan integrantes de la Convención Constitucional, entre ellos tres mujeres indígenas, y personas que filmaron las calles con imágenes que nunca llegaron a la prensa oficial.


Larraín, ciega y residente en Toronto, dejó Chile tras el golpe de Estado de 1973. Comenzó a perder la vista durante el montaje de un documental anterior. Su primer largometraje independiente fue El Juicio de Pascual Pichun (2007), que retrata la historia de dos familias, la del lonko Pascual Pichun y la del terrateniente Agustín Figueroa, en lo que se conoció como uno de los juicios más emblemáticos de la historia de Chile. Su obra posterior incluye Niña Sombra (2016), sobre los vendedores ambulantes ciegos de la Alameda.


“Esta película es mi respuesta. Un homenaje a quienes perdieron la vida defendiendo un proceso transformador que me marcó para siempre”, afirma la directora.


Estrenada en 2025, Cuerpos en Crisis obtuvo el Premio a Mejor Film de la Diáspora en el Toronto International Nollywood Film Festival 2025, donde además fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Canadá, y fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Derechos Humanos en el Montreal Independent Film Festival 2026.


Tras su paso por Toronto y México, la película recorre Chile antes de su lanzamiento oficial en Sala K de Santiago el 27 de noviembre. En la región, además de Temuco, se exhibirá el 6 de noviembre en Saavedra (Ruka y Huerto Llelliuken, con integrantes de la comunidad mapuche KOLWE) y el 7 en Curarrehue (Aldea Intercultural Trawupeyüm).
